english.html: ressing him by infinite lascivious and immodest means. And if one further seeks the cause why children sometimes resemble their fathers and at other times their mothers: I shall say with the Philosopher that if the virtue of the man is more abundant, the child will take after the father; and on the contrary, if the seed of the woman prevails, the child will take the form and likeness of the mother; and if there is an equal quantity of seed, it will resemble both, though in different places and parts of the body <sup class="mk" data-key="n">n</sup>. From which opinion Anaxagoras did not depart greatly when he said that the child will resemble that one of the parents who has contributed more seed.

notes.citation: Aristotle, Generation of Animals (IV.3, on resemblance to the father or mother)
notes.original: Ariſtote au liure de la generation des animaux.
notes.gloss: The closing sentence on Anaxagoras carries no marker.

english.html: Wherefore there was no cause for astonishment if the supplicant, incredibly desirous of seeing and recovering her husband.

The chaste and modest wife who truly loves her husband has nothing so dear nor so precious as his presence, and nothing so grievous and lamentable as his absence: witness the sad laments that one reads in Ovid a, of Penelope (true portrait and exemplar of chastity) for her Ulysses, of Hermione for her Orestes, of Deianira for her Hercules, and above all of Laodamia for her Protesilaus, whose absence she so deplored that, having afterwards heard that he had been slain by Hector, seized with an extreme frenzy and impatience, she went out of the bounds of reason [unclear: the print reads hors des gens de raison, perhaps for hors des gonds de raison, "off the hinges of reason"] and, as one transported, no longer wishing to live, asked of the gods, as the sole comfort and relief of her grief, that she might see the spirit of her departed love. Which she obtained, and in the arms of that shade gave up the ghost. And there is no doubt that the sovereign desire of one who loves is to see and contemplate the thing loved, for the great and incredible pleasure which he expects in seeing it; whence love in Greek is called ἐρῶς (erōs): for from the look love is born and takes its cause, and of it the eyes, as Propertius says, are the guides, chiefs and conductors b.

notes.citation: Ovid, Heroides I (Penelope to Ulysses), VIII (Hermione to Orestes), IX (Deianira to Hercules), XIII (Laodamia to Protesilaus)
notes.gloss: Laodamia's death in the arms of her husband's shade is not in Ovid's letter, which is written before the news; it is the version of Hyginus, Fabulae 103–104, and Servius on Aeneid VI.447.
